newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia okays 2nd stage in Earth's invasion of Mars.
newsitem.headline: Russia okays 2nd stage in Earth's invasion of Mars.

text.p: Russian space officials gave their $64 million mission to Mars a final green light on Monday and said the six-tonne probe would blast off on a 10-month mission on Saturday.

It's the next stage of Earth's invasion of Mars which began last Thursday when the U.S. launched the first of three robot missions to the Red Planet, target of intense speculation whether life exists or once existed there.
Russia is running the second interplanetary trek, followed by another U.S. probe to be fired next month.
Yuri Milov, deputy head of the Russian space agency, told a news conference that the Mars-96 probe had been attached to a booster rocket at the Baikonur cosmodrome in Kazakhstan.
"In two days they will be carried to the launch pad for final tests," he said.
Mars-96 will carry 1.1 tonnes of scientific equipment from 20 European countries and the United States to the Red Planet.
But cost constraints mean there will be no back-up probe if things go wrong.
"We hope the probe will reach Mars on September 12 next year," Stanislav Kulikov, chief designer at the Lavochkin scientific production space centre which built Mars-96.
The probe includes two special drilling devices to bore up to five metres (16 feet) into the surface of the planet, beaming information back to the orbiting probe.
The flight was originally scheduled for 1994, but was postponed due to cash shortages.
Milov said Russia had spent 350 billion roubles ($64 million) over two years to prepare for the mission. "Almost all the money came from the state budget," he said.
The U.S. space agency sent its Mars Global Surveyor off last week.
The one-tonne spacecraft replaced NASA's $1 billion Mars Observer probe, which spun out of control just days before it was due to enter orbit around the Red Planet in 1993.
Surveyor has identical copies of five of the seven scientific instruments on its ill-fated predecessor, but at $215 million is much cheaper.

From an altitude of 230 miles (367 km) its telephoto camera will see objects on the surface as small as a compact car. By the end of one Martian year -- or 687 Earth days -- 99 percent of the planet will have been mapped by Surveyor's electronic eye.
Other instruments will determine the composition of the Martian surface and attempt to detect traces of water, an essential ingredient for life.
The Russian launch will be followed by the second U.S. probe, Mars Pathfinder, on Dec 2.
